en: The *Gītagovinda* poem composed by Śrī Jayadeva Gosvāmī;
the *Śrī Gītagovinda* poem (1).
The sky is thick with clouds; the forest lands are dark with tamāla trees; and this night is fearful for one who is timid. Therefore, O Rādhā, you yourself must lead him home.
Thus, as Rādhā and Mādhava set out at Nanda’s command, may their secret amours by the banks of the Yamunā—occurring at every tree in the groves along the way—be ever victorious.

The poet Jayadeva composes this musical composition, which is joined with the accounts of the amorous dalliances of Śrī Vāsudeva; he whose inner dwelling is adorned by the deeds of the Goddess of Speech, and who is the sovereign of the bards at the feet of Padmāvatī. (GG 1.2)
If your mind is full of longing for the remembrance of Hari, and if you have a curiosity for the arts of graceful play,
then listen to the speech of Jayadeva, whose verses consist of sweet, soft, and beautiful lines.
Umāpatidhara causes his speech to sprout like a tender leaf; Jayadeva alone knows the purity of composition in words; Śaraṇa is the praiseworthy refuge for the difficult-to-comprehend and the swift;
but there is no one renowned who rivals the teacher Govardhana in the arrangement of excellent themes preeminent in the erotic sentiment—that bearer of tradition, the king of poets, Dhoyī. (GG 1.4)
The First Chapter.
It is sung in the Mālava-Gauḍa rāga with the Rūpaka tāla: the Aṣṭāpadī.
In the waters of the ocean at the time of dissolution, you bore the Veda, which had undertaken the practice of being a ship, without weariness;
O Keśava, who assumed the body of a fish, victory to you, O Lord of the World, O Hari! [The Refrain] GG_1.5 (1.1)
The earth rests upon your exceedingly vast back, which is heavy with the circles of calluses from supporting the world;
O Keśava, who assumed the form of a tortoise, victory to you, Lord of the Universe, Hare!
The earth clings to the tip of your tusk, submerged like a speck of darkness upon the moon.
O Keśava, who assumed the form of a boar, victory to you, O Lord of the world, Hare!

(1.3) Upon your excellent lotus-hand, the nail is a wondrous horn that crushed the bee-like body of Hiraṇyakaśipu; O Keśava, who assumed the form of Nṛsiṃha, victory to you, O Lord of the world, Hare! (1.4)

O Keśava, who assumed the form of Vāmana, you who purify the people with the water from the toenails of your wondrous dwarf-foot, you deceive Bali in your stride; victory to You, O Hare, Lord of the World! (1.9) You bathe the world—freed from sin and with the heat of worldly existence stilled—in the waters consisting of the blood of the Kṣatriyas.
O Keśava, who assumed the form of the Lord of the Bhṛgus, victory to You, O Lord of the World, Hare!
In battle, You bestowed upon the quarters of space that which was desirable even to the Guardians of the Quarters—[the head] of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, beautiful as an offering;
O Keśava, who assumed the body of Rāma, victory to You, O Lord of the World, Hare!

NOTE: {The reading in the Ha-saṃskaraṇa manuscript is "raghupati-rūpaṃ."} You wear upon your fair body a garment with the luster of a cloud, appearing like the Yamunā when she was joined [with you] out of fear of the blow of your plow.
O Keśava, who have assumed the form of the wielder of the plow! Victory to You, O Lord of the World, O Hari! (1.12) (1.8)
Alas! You, whose heart is compassionate, censure the Vedic tradition which ordains sacrifice and displays the slaughter of animals.
O Keśava, who assumed the body of Buddha, victory to you, O Lord of the world, O Hare! (1.13) To slay the multitudes of barbarians, you wield a sword as formidable as a comet.
O Keśava, who have assumed the body of Kalki, victory to you, O Lord of the world, Hare!
(10) Listen to this noble utterance of the poet Śrī Jayadeva, which bestows happiness, bestows auspiciousness, and is the very essence of existence:
O Keśava, who have assumed the tenfold forms, victory to you, O Lord of the world, Hare! (11) * * * * *

Salutations to You, Kṛṣṇa, who assumes ten forms: who retrieves the Vedas, sustains the worlds, upholds the earth, shatters the Daitya [Pralamba], deceives Bali, effects the destruction of the Kṣatriyas, conquers the son of Pulastya [Rāvaṇa], wields the plow, extends compassion, and stupefies the Mlecchas. (1.16) (5) // Book 2 //
It is sung in the *gurjarī* rāga and the *niḥsāra* tāla:
O You who have taken refuge in the circle of Lakṣmī’s breasts, who wear earrings,
and who are adorned with a beautiful forest garland!
Victory, victory to you, O Lord Hari!
[The Refrain: O ornament of the orb of the sun,
the destroyer of worldly existence!
O swan of the minds of the sages, victory, victory to you, O Lord Hari! GG_1.18 //
O vanquisher of the serpent Kāliya,
delighter of the people,
sun for the lotus of the Yadu clan!
Victory, victory to you, O Lord Hari!
O destroyer of Madhu, Mura, and Naraka;
O Lord who has Garuḍa as His seat;
O source of the divine pastimes of the celestial hosts!
Victory, victory to you, O Lord Hari!
O You with eyes like pure lotus petals,
O Deliverer from worldly existence,
O Treasure of the three worlds!
Victory, victory to you, O Lord Hari!
O you who adorned yourself with the ornaments made by Janaka’s daughter,
who conquered Dūṣaṇa,
and who quelled the Ten-necked one in battle!
Victory, victory to you, O Lord Hari!
O you who are as beautiful as a fresh rain-cloud,
who held Mount Mandara, and who are the cakora bird for the moon of Your glorious face!
Victory, victory to you, O Lord Hari!
We bow at your feet;
consider us thus.
Bestow welfare upon those who bow before you;
victory, victory, O Lord Hari!
This auspicious, radiant song by the poet Śrī Jayadeva brings joy to this [heart].
Victory, victory to you, O Lord Hari!
May the chest of Madhusūdana— marked by saffron paste from its embrace with the slopes of Padmā’s breasts,
as if manifesting his passion with a flood of perspiration born from the fatigue of amorous play— fulfill your desire.

In the spring, as Rādhā wandered through the forest with limbs as delicate as vāsantī blossoms, having pursued Kṛṣṇa for a long time, her companion spoke these words to her with pathos, seeing her suffering from the intense agitation of anxiety born of the fever of love. (GG 1.27)
NOTE: {“calat” is an alternative reading.} // Section 3 //
It is sung in the *vasanta-rāga*, with the *yati* and *tāla* meters:
In the Malaya breeze, tender from its caressing of the graceful *lavaṅga* creeper;
in the bower-cottage of the grove, filled with the warbling of cuckoos mingled with swarms of bees. (GG 1.28)
Hari dwells here in this springtime full of essence;
O friend, he dances together with the young women—this which is difficult for those separated from their lovers to endure. (Dhr)

In the midst of the lamentations produced by the wives of travelers whose desires were maddened by love, amidst the clusters of bakula trees where the masses of flowers were swarming with swarms of bees; GG_1.29 //

In this grove of tamāla trees, where the fresh leaf-garlands are submissive to the intensity of the musk's fragrance, and which, like a cluster of kiṃśuka flowers, possesses the luster of the nails of the Mind-born God as he tears open the hearts of young men; GG_1.30.

When the filaments of the *kesara* flowers bloomed with the luster of King Madana’s golden staff, they displayed the grace of Cupid’s quiver, filled with a mass of bees whose faces were as red as *pāṭala* blossoms.
O you who have brought forth a youthful smile with a glance that dispels the shame of the world;
O you whose horizon is bristling with *ketaka* flowers shaped like the points of spears that cut through those separated from their lovers!

O youth, [these breezes] are charming with the fragrance of *mādhavikā* flowers, sweetly scented with fresh *mālatī* and *jāti*, and they enchant even the minds of sages. (Note: There is an alternative reading, *mālikayātisugandhau*.)
—The bondage of the instruments of action. // GG_1.33 //

In the forest grove of Vṛndāvana, purified by the waters of the Yamunā flowing along its borders, where the mango trees have blossomed and bristled with horripilation from the embrace of the quivering atimukta vines; GG_1.34.

This description of the forest in the season of the flavorful spring, spoken by Śrī Jayadeva— whose essence is the remembrance of Hari’s feet and which follows the transformations of love— is now dawning.
* * * * * It perfumes the groves with the manifest scents of cloth-fragrances produced by the shimmering pollen of jasmine creepers broken apart by gentle breezes.
For here, indeed, this wind—which is the kinsman of the fragrance of the ketaki flower and possesses the power of the spreading, peerless arrows [of the god of love]—burns the heart.

NOTE: {In this edition accompanied by the commentary of Haridāsadāsa’s Prabodhānanda, verse number 48 is seen:} "Tormented in the ears by the clamor of the warbling cuckoos sporting among mango sprouts shaken by bees greedy for the scent of emerging honey;
NOTE: {There is an alternative reading: "kala-ravaiḥ" (by sweet sounds).}"
How, by what means, are these days passed by travelers, who find a momentary surge of joy in the union of their vital breaths attained through the concentration of meditation?

Pointing out Murāri from nearby— He who is intensely eager for the charming amorous play that throbs with the agitation of embracing many women— a certain female companion spoke again to Rādhikā in the presence of her friends.
// Narrative 4 //
It is sung in the Rāmakarī rāga, with yati and tāla meters:

He whose dark-blue body is anointed with sandalwood paste, who wears yellow garments and a forest garland, whose pair of cheeks is adorned with jeweled earrings swaying in play, and who possesses a radiant smile. (GG 1.39)
O playful one, Hari sports here among this multitude of charming young wives who are intent on amorous play. (Dhr)
Embracing Hari with the weight of her full breasts,
a certain cowherd maiden, filled with passion, sang along with him, raising the *pañcama* melody.

A certain charming young woman meditates intensely upon the lotus-face of Madhusūdana, which has surpassed the god of love produced by the playful movement of her own eyes, restless with amorous charm.
A certain woman with beautiful hips, leaning against his cheek and whispering something at the root of his ear, kissed her beloved— who was made favorable by horripilation— sweetly.
And out of curiosity for the arts of play, a certain woman on the banks of the Yamunā pulled him by his silken garment with her hand as he had entered a lovely grove of *vañjula* trees.

In the delight of the *rāsa* dance, a young woman, intent on dancing together with Hari to the sweet sound of the flute— which was resonating with the jingling of her rows of bracelets trembling against her palms— was praised by him.
He embraces one woman, kisses another, delights yet another beautiful lady,
gazes with a charming smile at a fourth, and follows after a fifth who is lovely.
May this wonderful secret of Keśava’s pastimes, spoken by Śrī Jayadeva and charmingly performed in the forest of Vṛndāvana, spread auspiciousness and glory. (GG 1.46)

NOTE: {The reading "valitam" is also found.} * * * * * O friend, in the springtime, Hari—bringing joy to all by his pleasing ways, creating a festival for the God of Love with limbs as dark and tender as a row of blue lotuses, and embraced on every limb from all sides by the beautiful women of Vraja at his own will—sports like the personified embodiment of erotic passion (śṛṅgāra), charming in his beauty. GG_1.47 //
As if distressed by the torment of being swallowed by the serpent dwelling upon its own lap, the breeze from the sandalwood mountain pursues Mount Īśācala with a desire for a plunge into its snow;
moreover, beholding the buds at the tops of the succulent mango trees, the cries of the cuckoos— sweet, exalted, and warbling "kuhū, kuhū"— break forth out of rising joy.

NOTE: {This verse was not read by Prabodhānanda} May Hari protect you—he who, having closely embraced the chest of the beautiful-browed cowherd girls who were filled with amorous play through the intensity of their delight in the *rāsa* dance, was kissed passionately by Rādhā—who was blinded by love—under the pretext of singing praises, as she exclaimed, "Excellent! Your face is composed of nectar," while he himself captivated her with his smile. GG_1.49 //
NOTE: {smṛta (?)}.
Thus ends the first canto, titled "The Joyful Dāmodara," in the illustrious *Gītagovinda*.
(2) The second canto.
Free from the distress of jealousy,
Rādhā dwelt in the forest with Hari, whose love was shared by all; yet, having departed elsewhere out of envy born from her own vanishing sense of superiority,
she— though miserable and hidden in a certain bower of creepers where the tops were resonant with swarms of humming bees— spoke in secret to her friend.
// Narrative 5 //
It is sung in the Gurjari raga with the Yati rhythm:
The enchanting flute resounds with the sweet sound of the nectar from his moving lips;
his crest-jewel and ear-ornament sway upon his cheeks as his side-glances flicker.
My mind remembers Hari performing his pastimes here at the rāsa-dance, where he engaged in playful jests. (Dhruva-pada) GG_2.2 //
His hair was encircled by a halo like the beautiful crest of a peacock with its moon-like eye;
his fine attire was like a thick rain cloud colored by the many-arched bow of Indra.

Her lips, like the tender sprouts of the *bandhujīva* flower, were beautiful with a radiant smile and possessed a luster gained from kissing the faces of the cowherd maidens whose hips were like those of the *kadamba* tree.
Surrounded by thousands of cowherd maidens whose sprout-like arms were bristling with intense horripilation,
the darkness was dispelled by the rays from the clusters of jewel-ornaments upon their hands, feet, and chests.
Her forehead is adorned with a sandalwood tilaka that mocks the moon moving behind a mass of clouds;
her heart is as firm as a door-panel, merciless in its crushing embrace of the slopes of her full breasts.
His noble cheeks were adorned with earrings as enchanting as jeweled makaras;
he wore yellow garments and was surrounded by an excellent retinue of sages, humans, gods, and asuras.
He was gathered beneath a bright kadamba tree, quelling the fear of the defilements of the Kali age;
he delighted even me with a mind whose glance was like a shimmering wave of passion.

The form of the enemy of Madhu (Kṛṣṇa), which is exceedingly beautiful and enchanting, as described by Śrī Jayadeva, is now worthy of those who possess merit for the purpose of remembering the feet of Hari. He counts the multitude of virtues; he does not even desire the splendor of anger arising from delusion; he carries satisfaction everywhere and casts faults far away.
NOTE: O Kṛṣṇa, who sport among young women with your ever-turning thirst, my perverse mind desires you once again even without me; what can I do? (GG 2.10)
// Narrative 6 //
It is sung in the Mālava-gauḍa rāga and the Ekatālī tāla:
Having gone at night to a secluded bower-house, she hid herself while He was dwelling there;
with all directions gazed upon in alarm, He laughed out of the intensity of the passion for amorous play. (GG 2.11)
O friend, delight the noble crusher of Keśin with me, who am filled with the longing of love, in a state of passionate agitation. (This is the refrain.)
Shy at their first meeting, she made herself favorable with hundreds of clever flatteries;
with her soft, sweet smiles and speech, she loosened the silk garment from her hips.
Having lain for a long time upon my very chest while she rested on a bed of young shoots,
she embraced me, performed kisses, and drank from my lower lip.
With eyes half-closed in languor, her cheeks graced by a line of horripilation,
and her entire body drenched in the sweat of exertion, she was exceedingly restless from the intoxication of supreme passion.
With her cooing of sweet warbling like that of a cuckoo, she surpassed the contemplation of the science of love;
with her locks disheveled by loose flowers, she bore the weight of her firm breasts marked by nail-scratches.
With her jeweled anklets tinkling at her feet, she filled the canopy of their lovemaking;
with her jingling, loosened girdle, she gave herself up to kisses accompanied by the seizing of her hair.
With her lotus-eyes slightly closed in languor from the savor of the occasion of amorous pleasure,
her slender vine-like body collapsed helplessly as she gazed upon Madhusūdana, who had awakened the god of love within her.
May this work, composed by Śrī Jayadeva, which possesses the nature of the supreme amorous pastimes of the Enemy of Madhu,
and which was joyfully recounted by the longing cowherd women, spread playful delight.

[The Lord] whose flute slipped from His hand, whose creeper-like eyebrows were arched, who was gazed upon by the sidelong glances of the multitude of cowherd women, and whose cheeks were moist with excessive perspiration...
Beholding Govinda, whose forest-like face is charming with the nectar of his smile, surrounded by the hosts of beautiful women of Vraja, I look upon him with shame and yet I rejoice. GG_2.19 //
The breeze from the lake’s grove causes pain even as it causes the new clusters of blossoms on the *aśoka* creepers—creepers difficult to behold—to bloom;
and yet, O friend, this mountain peak does not bring joy, for the mango trees there produce buds that are charming only with the humming of wandering bees.

May the ever-new Keśava remove your affliction—he who, having secretly observed the gopīs with a meaningful smile, their hair disheveled and falling, their creeper-like brows uplifted, and the half of their breasts revealed by the roots of their arms as they playfully displayed them; he who, his longing satisfied, has long been contemplating that enchanting beauty within his mind. (GG 2.21)
Thus ends the second canto, named "Keśava Without Effort," in the great poem Śrī Gītagovinda.
(3) The Third Canto.
Even Madhusūdana,
the enemy of Kaṃsa, was captivated by the fetters bound by the latent impressions of worldly existence.
Having placed Rādhā in his heart, he abandoned the beauties of Vraja.
Having searched for Rādhikā here and there, his mind exhausted by the wounds of Cupid’s arrows and filled with remorse,
Mādhava despaired within a bower on the bank of the Yamunā.
// Narrative 7 //
It is sung in the Gurjari raga, with yati and tala meters:
"Seeing that she had departed while surrounded by a multitude of young women, I did not stop her out of great fear, even though I was at fault. (GG 3.3)
Alas, alas! She has gone away as if angry, having lost all regard for me.
The fixed state.
What will she do, what will she say after such a long separation?
What is the use of wealth, of people, of life, or of my home to me?
I think of her face with its arched brows and its weight of anger,
like a red lotus above which a restless bee is hovering.
I take constant and intense delight in her who dwells within my heart;
why then do I pursue her in the forest, and why do I lament here in vain?
O slender one, I perceive your heart is distressed by resentment;
yet I do not know where you have gone, and for that reason, I do not offer you my entreaties.
You appear before me, yet you perform only coming and going;
why do you not grant me an embrace with the same eagerness as before?
"Forgive me; never again shall I act in such a manner toward you.
O beautiful one, grant me your sight, for I am tormented by the god of love."
This [hymn] of Hari has been described by Jayadeva, who is bowed down [in devotion],
the lover of Rohiṇī, who was born from the ocean of the Kindubilva clan. (GG 3.10)
The necklace upon my heart is a lotus-stalk fiber, not the lord of serpents; the cluster of blue-lotus petals around my neck is not the luster of poison;
this is sandalwood dust, not ashes. O Anaṅga, do not strike me—who am bereft of my beloved—with the delusion that I am Hara; why do you rush toward me in such wrath?
"Do not take up this mango-arrow in your hand, nor string your bow; O conqueror of the universe through play, what manliness is there in striking people into a swoon?
For even now, the mind of that very fawn-eyed girl—shattered by the volley of glances from her darting side-long looks—is not the least bit restored."

Did Smara place upon her—the moving deity who has conquered the bodiless one—all those weapons that have vanquished the world: her sprout-like eyebrows as the bow, the undulations of her outer corners as the arrows, and the curve of her ear as the string? (GG 3.13)
The side-glance, like an arrow set upon the bow of her brow, shall pierce my vital organs; let even the dark and curling mass of her hair bring about my destruction.
O slender one, let this red-lipped bimba-fruit of hers cause my delusion; but how can your breast-circle—though well-rounded and possessed of passion—play with my life-breaths?

Those pleasures of touch, those tremulous and tender playfulnesses of her eyes, that fragrance of her lotus-face, that sweetness of her speech flowing like nectar, and that loveliness of her bimba-fruit lips— if the mind remains fixed in meditative absorption upon her even while engaged with these sensory objects, alas, how can the disease of separation increase?

May the waves of sidelong glances from the moon-like face of Rādhā—waves which, though unnoticed by hundreds of thousands of women intent on the notes of the flute-song rising from the bamboo, as their heads swayed and their crest-jewels trembled—long bestow upon you well-being; for they sprang forth from that essence of nectar, the sweet and enchanting countenance of Madhusūdana. (GG 3.16)
Thus ends the third canto, titled "The Bewildered Madhusūdana," in the great poem *Śrī Gītagovinda*.
(4) The Fourth Canto.
In a grove of *vānīra* reeds on the banks of the Yamunā, Rādhikā’s friend spoke softly to Mādhava, who was languidly seated there, his mind overwhelmed by the weight of love. (GG 4.1)
// Narrative 8 //

It is sung in the Karṇāṭa rāga and the Eka-tālī tāla: She censures sandalwood paste, finds distress at the touch of the moonbeams, and regards the Malaya breeze as if it were poison because of its contact with the abode of serpents. (GG 4.2)
O Mādhava, as if out of fear of the arrows of the mind-born god, she has merged into you through meditative absorption;
for she is wretched in separation from you.
The fixed state.
As if from the incessant falling of the arrows of Love, she places a shield over the vital spot of her own heart— a broad lattice of water-laden lotus petals— to protect herself from you.
This bed of flowers, lovely with its many arts of grace, acts as a couch for the arrows of the flower-arrowed god; it serves as a vow, as it were, for the sake of the pleasure of your embrace.
And she bears her noble lotus-face with its flowing stream of moving glances,
like the moon shedding streams of nectar when it is being bitten by the fangs of the monstrous Rāhu.
In secret, she draws you—become the embodiment of the peerless arrow—with musk from the deer;
she bows to the sea-monster while holding beneath her hand an arrow made of fresh mango blossoms.
Having first visualized you— who are exceedingly difficult to attain— within the state of meditative absorption,
she laments, laughs, desponds, weeps, trembles, and releases her fever.
Mādhava, at every step she declares this as well: "I have fallen at your feet;
when you turn your face away from me, even the ocean of nectar instantly spreads a burning heat throughout my body."
If this, spoken by Śrī Jayadeva, is deemed sufficient, let it be danced;
otherwise, let the words of the friend of the young cowherd girl, distressed by separation from Hari, be recited:
"The forest acts as her dwelling, even the garland of her dear friend acts as a snare, and the heat of her sighing becomes a mass of flames from a forest fire."
Alas! In separation from you, she too, O woe, acts like a doe; and how is it that even the God of Love acts like Yama, performing his "tiger's play"? (GG 4.10)
// Narrative 9 //
It is sung in the *deśākhyarāga* and the *ekatālītāla* meters:
"Though the magnificent necklace is placed upon her breasts, that slender-bodied woman regards it as a burden. (GG 4.11)
O Keśava, Rādhikā [is suffering] in separation from you; this is certain.
Even the fragrant and smooth sandalwood paste on his body he looks upon with apprehension, as if it were poison.
It carries the wind of her sighing, which possesses an incomparable expansion,
like the fire of passion that burns with feverish heat.
In every direction it scatters a web of water droplets,
like a lotus of the eye from which the stalk has slipped away.
She does not leave her cheek from the palm of her hand,
as if she were gazing at the steady young moon in the evening.
Even a bed of tender sprouts, though it falls within the range of her vision,
she perceives as being filled with the dread of fire.
She chants "Hari, Hari" according to her desire,
as if she were intent on dying due to the pain of separation.

May this song, composed by Śrī Jayadeva and offered at the feet of Keśava, grant you happiness. (GG 4.18) She experiences horripilation, utters sighs of pleasure, laments, trembles, faints, meditates, wanders in delusion, closes her eyes in bliss, falls down, rises again, and even faints away.

O you whose body is like that of the celestial physician, if you were to show favor out of compassion, would this fair-bodied one not live even in such intense fever? Otherwise, her hand has already been surrendered.

O Physician of the Gods, you do not restore Rādhā—who is afflicted by love and can be cured solely by the nectar of contact with your limbs—to freedom from her suffering; thus, you are more cruel than even the thunderbolt of Upendra.

It is a marvel that the mind of this woman, whose body is afflicted by the feverish torment of the god of love, has long been wasting away in anxious thoughts of sandalwood, the moon, and lotus ponds;

yet, though she stands alone in solitude and somehow survives with her strength exhausted, it is only through the power of exhaustion that she breathes for a moment while meditating upon you alone—the beloved whose very form is cool.
How can she, who formerly could not endure separation from you for even a moment— being distressed by the closing of her eyes—
now breathe at all upon seeing the mango branch with its flowering tip after such a long parting?

May the arm of the enemy of Kaṃsa— the arm that lifted Govardhana out of its love for the forest of Gokula which was distressed by the rain, and which, while bearing the mountain, was long kissed with great joy by the beloved wives of the cowherds, and which bears the imprint of the vermilion from the edge of their lips as if out of pride— may that arm of the body of the cowherd extend blessings to you all.
Thus ends the fourth canto, named *Snigdha-madhusūdana*, in the illustrious *Gītagovinda*.
(5) The Fifth Canto.
"O lotus-eyed one, I dwell here full of longing; go, entreat Rādhā with my words and bring her back. Thus commanded by Madhuripu, the friend went herself and spoke this again to Rādhā.
// Narrative 10 //
It is sung in the Deśīvarāḍī rāga and the Rūpaka tāla:
When the Malaya breeze blows, bringing with it the god of love, the clusters of flowers burst open for the purpose of shattering the hearts of those separated from their lovers. (GG 5.2)
In separation from you, O friend, the wearer of the forest garland languishes; this is the firm conclusion.
He is burned by the cool-rayed moon; he imitates death;
he falls under the arrow of Love; and, utterly distraught, he laments.
When the swarm of bees hums, she covers her ears;
when separation is felt in her mind, she suffers pain night after night.
He dwells under the canopy of the forest, he abandons his graceful abode;
he rolls upon the bed of the earth and repeatedly utters your name.

The poet Jayadeva says: By the play of separation, through the power of his own merit, may Hari arise in the heart of her whose passion is intense. In that very bower—a great sacred ford for the god of love—where formerly the master of passion attained his perfections together with you, Mādhava [now dwells] once again.
Constantly meditating upon you and even muttering the series of mantras that are your very words, he still yearns for the nectar of the intense embrace of your jar-like breasts.
// Narrative 11 //
In the Gurjari raga and Ekatali tal, it is sung:
"O woman of broad hips, do not delay your departure; follow that lord of your heart, who has gone to the trysting place for the essence of the pleasure of love, wearing a dress enchanting to Madana."

In the forest on the bank of the Yamunā, where a gentle breeze blows, dwells the one who wears a forest garland, his two hands restless with the massaging of the slopes of her full breasts. (Dhrupada)
